title: Adolescence, Adulthood, Interpersonal Relationships and Old Age
introduction: Spanning the biological surge of puberty through early adulthood's pragmatic specialization, midlife's climacteric transitions and relationship arcs, and late adulthood's quest for integrity and wisdom, the second half of the lifespan illustrates that human growth continues until death. Developmental psychologists play vital supportive roles across adolescent turmoil, adult relationships, and healthy aging.
learningOutcomes: 8.1 Distinguish primary from secondary sexual characteristics in adolescence and describe adolescent formal-operational cognition, four psychosocial tasks, and internalizing versus externalizing disorders.
8.2 Describe physical, cognitive (relativistic and pragmatic thinking), and social transitions during Early Adulthood (19–35 years).
8.3 Explain Middle Adulthood (35–60 years) changes, including the climacteric (menopause and male hormonal decline) and Crystallized versus Fluid intelligence.
8.4 Detail George Levinger's five-stage (ABCDE) Model of Relationships and explain the role of developmental psychologists in supporting adult relationships.
8.5 Analyze physical, cognitive (memory, wisdom, plasticity/training), and psychosocial (Integrity vs. Despair) aspects of Old Age (60+ years), distinguishing primary from secondary aging factors.

content.heading: Adolescence: Puberty, Complex Cognition, Psychosocial Tasks, and Vulnerability
content.body: Adolescence marks the transition from puberty (onset of sexual maturity and reproductive capacity) to adulthood, driven by pituitary-stimulated estrogens and androgens producing rapid growth spurts—by the end of adolescence, 98% of adult height is achieved (cited norms note ~36 cm/25 kg gains in boys and ~24 cm/21 kg in girls across ages 10–19). Biological pubertal changes divide into Primary Sexual Characteristics (directly tied to reproduction and primary sex organs: ovulation and menstruation in girls; semen production in boys) and Secondary Sexual Characteristics (visible outward traits: breast development in girls, facial beard in boys, and underarm/pubic hair in both sexes). Cognitively, adolescents enter Formal Logical Operations—thinking abstractly and hypothetically (contrary-to-fact scenarios), debating global ideas (justice, politics, history, patriotism), and often displaying idealism or temporary intolerance of opposing views. Psychosocially, adolescents navigate Erikson's Identity vs. Role Confusion (ages 12–18) across four core developmental tasks needed for healthy adulthood: (1) Independence, (2) Body Image, (3) Peer Relations, and (4) Identity. Influenced heavily by home and school environments, hormonal and social upheaval creates vulnerability to Psychosocial Problems categorized as Internalizing Disorders (depression, anxiety) and Externalizing Disorders (delinquency, aggression, educational difficulties, truancy). Developmental psychologists support teens using psychosocial skills training: social problem-solving, role-playing, supervised interactions, didactic instruction, modelling, and reinforcement.

content.heading: Early Adulthood (19–35 Years) and Middle Adulthood (35–60 Years)
content.body: Early Adulthood (19–35 years) centres on solidifying intimate, marital, family, and career roles. While gross physical growth ends in the teens, muscle strength, reaction time, and sensory acuity peak in the 20s before beginning slow age-related declines in the mid-30s (e.g., eye lens losing flexibility, weakening tooth-supporting tissues). Cognitively, functioning stabilizes and peaks around age 35, shifting from rigid right-vs.-wrong views to Relativistic Thinking (recognizing multiple perspectives and answers) and Pragmatic Thinking (applying logic to real-world problems while accepting contradiction and imperfection), boosted by educational or career expertise. Middle Adulthood (35–60 years) introduces noticeable gradual declines in muscle strength, digestive/circulatory performance, and the reproductive Climacteric: menopause (cessation of menses in late 40s/early 50s) in women, and reduced sex hormones and prostate function lowering sexual drive in men. Cognitively, short-term memory remains stable while long-term recall dips mildly, and intelligence is analysed in two forms: Crystallized Intelligence (accumulated lifetime knowledge, skills, and strategies—holds steady or IMPROVES into the mid-50s and beyond, complemented by rising practical problem-solving, wisdom, and creativity) versus Fluid Intelligence (basic information-processing speed, divided attention, and rapid novel problem-solving—begins declining prior to or during midlife).

content.heading: Adulthood Relationships and George Levinger's Five-Stage (ABCDE) Model
content.body: Positive, meaningful relationships with spouses, children, parents, friends, and communities strongly bolster adult well-being (whereas failing to build meaningful ties triggers Erikson's Intimacy vs. Isolation crisis and loneliness). Psychologist George Levinger proposed the widely used five-stage (ABCDE) Model of Relationships—originally formulated for adult romantic partnerships and broadly applied to friendships: (1) A — Acquaintance / Acquaintanceship (initial contact shaped by proximity, first impressions, and prior ties; may remain casual indefinitely); (2) B — Build-up (growing trust, care, intimacy needs, compatibility, and shared goals/backgrounds); (3) C — Continuation (long, relatively stable mutual commitment—close friendship, romance, or marriage—sustained by ongoing growth and mutual trust); (4) D — Deterioration (optional troubled phase marked by boredom, resentment, reduced communication/self-disclosure, betrayal, or lost trust—either spiralling downward or resolved by rebuilding trust); and (5) E — Ending / Termination (final severing of relationship ties through breakup, death, or spatial separation). Developmental psychologists assist adults experiencing relationship breakdowns or isolation to rebuild communication, trust, and emotional resilience.

content.heading: Old Age (60+ Years): Aging Factors, Cognition, Wisdom, and Integrity vs. Despair
content.body: Old Age (60s to death—its subjective onset increasingly delayed by rising life expectancy and longer careers) brings challenges including retirement, declining physical fitness, chronic ill health, bereavement (spousal loss), and loneliness. Physically, metabolism shifts alongside wear-and-tear and genetic biological clocks; aging stems from Primary Aging Factors (intrinsic biological processes: decline/loss of cellular function, drop in cell numbers, oxidative damage, DNA modification, tissue damage, natural selection) and Secondary Aging Factors (modifiable external influences such as unhealthy lifestyle). Cognitively, empirical research refutes stereotypes of inevitable severe cognitive collapse: although older adults learn more slowly and experience short-term sensory-storage difficulties acquiring new facts (whereas distant long-term memories remain strong), they compensate with rich Wisdom (practical expert life knowledge). Furthermore, cognitive plasticity persists—even a few hours of training, repetition, puzzles, hobbies, reading, or computer learning measurably improve older adults' mental performance. Psychosocially, elderly adults confront Erikson's Integrity vs. Despair: viewing life as meaningful yields integrity and low death anxiety, whereas unresolved regret breeds despair—an arena where developmental psychologists provide vital coping and aging support.

inTextQuestions.question: What are the four psychosocial developmental tasks an adolescent must accomplish to become a well-adjusted adult?
inTextQuestions.answer: Independence, body image, peer relations, and identity.

inTextQuestions.question: Distinguish between Internalizing Disorders and Externalizing Disorders during adolescence.
inTextQuestions.answer: Internalizing disorders include depression and anxiety, whereas externalizing disorders include delinquency, aggression, educational difficulties, and truancy.

inTextQuestions.question: Compare Crystallized Intelligence and Fluid Intelligence during middle adulthood.
inTextQuestions.answer: Crystallized intelligence (accumulated lifetime knowledge, skills, and strategies) stays stable or even improves through midlife, whereas Fluid intelligence (basic information-processing speed and divided attention) begins declining prior to or during middle adulthood.

inTextQuestions.question: Name the five stages of George Levinger's ABCDE Model of Relationships in sequence.
inTextQuestions.answer: 1. Acquaintance (Acquaintanceship), 2. Build-up, 3. Continuation, 4. Deterioration, and 5. Ending (Termination).

saqs.question: Differentiate primary from secondary sexual characteristics in adolescents and describe two key features of adolescent cognitive development.
saqs.answer: Primary sexual characteristics directly involve reproduction and sex organs (ovulation/menstruation in girls; semen production in boys). Secondary characteristics are visible outward traits (breasts in girls, beards in boys, pubic/underarm hair in both). Cognitively, adolescents develop formal operational abstract/hypothetical thinking and grapple with global concepts (justice, politics) with idealism.

saqs.question: Describe Relativistic Thinking and Pragmatic Thinking in early adulthood (19–35 years) and explain what the 'climacteric' means in middle adulthood (35–60 years).
saqs.answer: Relativistic thinking moves beyond simplistic right/wrong views to examine issues from multiple angles; pragmatic thinking applies logic to real-world problems while accepting contradiction and imperfection. The climacteric refers to midlife reproductive/sexual declines—menopause (cessation of menstruation) in women and lowered sex hormones/prostate function reducing sexual drive in men.

saqs.question: Outline all five stages of George Levinger's Model of Relationships and explain how developmental psychologists help resolve relationship challenges.
saqs.answer: 1. Acquaintance (proximity/first impressions); 2. Build-up (growing trust, intimacy, compatibility); 3. Continuation (long-term stable commitment and mutual trust); 4. Deterioration (boredom, resentment, reduced disclosure, betrayal—or resolution); 5. Termination/Ending (breakup, death, or separation). Developmental psychologists help adults navigate intimacy crises, combat loneliness, rebuild communication/trust, and manage emotional difficulties.

saqs.question: Compare primary aging factors and secondary aging factors in old age, and explain why memory complaints in older adults do not mean general cognitive loss.
saqs.answer: Primary aging factors are intrinsic biological processes (cellular decline, drop in cell numbers, oxidative damage, DNA modification, tissue damage); secondary aging factors stem from modifiable habits like unhealthy lifestyles. Older adults' memory complaints mainly reflect short-term sensory storage of new data rather than long-term memory loss; wisdom compensates, and practice, reading, puzzles, hobbies, and brief training measurably improve mental scores.

saqs.question: Explain Erikson's Integrity vs. Despair crisis in old age and list four major life challenges older adults face.
saqs.answer: Older adults evaluate whether their lives were meaningful: positive appraisal yields integrity and low death anxiety, whereas regret and feeling unable to contribute yield despair. Four major challenges: retirement from active work, declining physical fitness/ill health, death of loved ones/spousal loss, and loneliness.
